The Commission found the Agency executing its new powers once the transition ended, and the Agency's 2025 report gives specifics: 196 supervisions and 121 decisions ordering violations to be removed. Application is real but weak: supervisions found low compliance, other laws are not fully aligned, the Commission records no progress in 2025, a lack of budgetary independence and a NATO transfer amendment, none of which is repeal or suspension. Article 122 in the unofficial translation (provisions 'cease to apply until' accession) contradicts all this evidence, looks like a translation fault and should be checked against the Macedonian text.

The law was adopted in February 2020 and took effect that month, but controllers and processors had an 18-month transition that ended in August 2021, when the Commission dates full application. Items saying it took effect in February 2020 therefore describe entry into force, not full application.

The law was adopted on 27 June 2025 and amended on 29 December 2025; it entered into force on the eighth day after publication on 4 July 2025 and was due to apply from 1 June 2026, but no later item confirms application or reports measures under it, and the security supervision reported for 2025 rests on the earlier law. By-laws were due within 15 months (October 2026) and operators have 18 months to align (January 2027), so that deadline has not yet passed. The Commission's May 2026 finding that the step is not achieved, with a grace period to 30 June 2026 whose outcome is not in the evidence, concerns alignment, and 'draft' or 'proposal' wording in GOV-2025-004-0172 and GOV-2026-002-0100 is historic rather than a conflict.

The Commission reports in November 2025 that the country adopted a long-term ICT strategy and action plan, and the strategy text says some activities began before formal adoption. The goals in the text are targets, so they do not show delivery. The link between the Commission's sentence and SMART/MK is inferred from timing and is for the analyst to confirm.

The plan remains valid, and measures have been carried out in part: the Commission records 5G expanding to Skopje and biannual Broadband Competence Office reports. Commission reports for 2021 and 2022 record delay, and the Office's own report finds most 5G goals met but none of the three measures on 100 Mbps subscriptions implemented. These sources describe different parts of the plan, so they do not conflict.

Sub-area wording on access to the labour market, which matches this issue, says no progress in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 report says there were no legislative developments. The 2025 screening finding of partial alignment is a first assessment of that kind and does not show a change.

What remains is equal treatment of EU workers in the law on access to the labour market, including an end to posts in private companies reserved for nationals. The foreigners law is itself the barrier, the 2025 amendment only renames bodies and the further amendments are only proposed with unknown content (all statuses are proposals; the two government items are machine translated, so capped at Medium), while the country's general ban on nationality discrimination is its own account and does not close the gap. The Commission's statement that the law makes no EU distinction conflicts with the country's account on quotas, which is reported and partly explained under RI-FMW-002.

A key recommendation on non-discrimination against EU workers is repeated in the 2020 to 2025 reports, and equal access is central to the chapter. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found in the evidence.

The change is legal and within the government's control, and the same law was amended in 2021 and 2025. Against that, six reports record no alignment and the requirement runs to the time of accession, so there is no evidence of past progress.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches; Commission items describe annual quotas and work permits unchanged from 2020 to 2025, and the 2025 seasonal work law leaves conditions for EU citizens to be specified. Permit counts (755 in 2021, some 8 900 in 2024) are not used as a trend, because the bases appear to differ: the 2021 figure sits beside 3 242 separate opinions in a machine-translated agency report, capped at Medium.

What remains is access for EU citizens without work permits or residence permits, with their explicit exclusion from quotas, and no responding intervention is linked (statuses are proposals). The confirmed contradiction stands: the Commission says the law does not distinguish EU citizens, while the country says quotas do not apply to them under a reciprocity agreement. Art. 5(2) point 1 of the 2015 law (machine translated, so capped at Medium, and used under LIM-0024) partly explains this, because it does exempt foreigners given equality under such an agreement, but it is conditional, no item identifies a concluded agreement or shows it applied, and the Commission still requires the exclusion.

Permits and quotas are central to the chapter, but they are named as requirements only in the 2024 report and the screening report, not in the annual key recommendation, which is why this is central with thin support. If the reviewers read the key recommendation on non-discrimination as covering permits and quotas, this would be High; the large item count is mostly the law's own text and did not count.

The change needs only national law, but it involves two laws and the interior and labour ministries and the Employment Agency, and an international organisation reports overlapping mandates between the laws. The law was amended in 2021 and 2025 without touching this requirement, and the proposed amendments have unknown content.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is part of the chapter and no sub-area wording matches. The finding that EU citizens cannot take public administration posts, apart from some in health and education, is unchanged in each report from 2020 to 2025.

What remains is limiting the restriction to posts involving public authority and the general interest of the State, in line with case law of the Court of Justice. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the existing exemptions for health and higher education are the country's account and are narrower than the requirement.

This is a repeated finding central to the chapter, but public sector posts are named as a requirement only in the screening report and not in an annual key recommendation. If the reviewers read 'in all sectors' in the 2023 to 2025 key recommendation as covering them, this would be High.

The work is national and depends on no outside party, but it requires a careful review of civil servant categories across the public service against case law. There is no evidence of past progress and no responding intervention.

Sub-area wording on EURES, which matches this issue, says no developments or measures in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the 2023 key recommendation still asks for alignment. The screening report's 'good level of preparation' sits in tension with these and with its own finding that no appointment system exists; it is the only rating of this kind, so I do not read it as improvement, and I report the tension rather than resolve it.

What remains is a legal system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies. The Commission credits good alignment on IT and structural levels, but every responding intervention is only proposed (these statuses are themselves proposals), with legislative amendments on a 2030 deadline and implementation at accession.

Alignment with EURES is named in the key recommendation in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and EURES is one of the chapter's main strands. The recommendation is a composite one, so the repetition is of one sentence and not of independent findings.

One lead body is planned and the IT and structural base is credited, which helps. However, no legal step has been reported in six years, the country's own timetable runs to 2030 and implementation is tied to accession.

The chapter scale was context only. The key recommendation to strengthen the Employment Service Agency is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, which sets the default, and the 2025 report says the previous recommendations were not implemented. Training took place in 2023 and the screening report calls capacity satisfactory, but no earlier rating exists to show a rise from.

What remains is updated EURES training after staff turnover, with connection of private employment agencies and later ESCO mapping. The Commission finds the main IT elements in place and capacity satisfactory, and capacity building and IT upgrades are proposed here as implemented while further strengthening is only proposed; all these statuses are proposals.

Agency capacity is named in the key recommendation in three reports, so the requirement is repeated. It is not central now, because the Commission finds capacity satisfactory and the IT elements in place.

The remaining work rests mainly with one agency, does not depend on other countries and builds on training and IT delivered before. Past capacity building is reported by the Commission, not only by the government.

The chapter scale was context only. The composite recommendation naming the European Labour Authority is nearly unchanged in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and the only direct findings, in the screening report, say national law is not aligned.

What remains is aligning national law with the regulation and preparing the State Labour Inspectorate for coordinated tasks. Both responses are only proposed for the medium term, and the implemented training does not align the law; these statuses are proposals.

The authority is named in a key recommendation in three reports, but only as part of a sentence mainly about the employment service. The direct support is one source and the issue is not central to the chapter.

Harmonisation is within national control and plans exist, but the plans only run in the medium term, with full implementation at accession. They also need institutional and procedural preparation by the labour inspectorate as well as legal change.

The chapter scale was context only, and the issue's EU items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read. The 2026 items are regional, concern migrant workers generally and cannot alone support a finding about the country.

What remains is designating an institution to support EU mobile workers and improving the system that informs them of their rights. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare.
The requirement appears in one report, in repeated sentences, and is not named in a key recommendation. The regional items do not raise this, as they concern other workers.

Designating an institution is a single national decision, with no dependence on others and few actors. There is no evidence of past progress, so this rests on the nature of the task and is less certain for the wider information system.

The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 'good level of preparation' for coordination is a single rating with nothing before it. No new agreements are recorded in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025, despite negotiations started in 2023. Two confirmed count contradictions stand (14 against 13 EU agreements; 23 against 22 in total); they do not change this view and are not resolved here.

What remains is agreements with the other Member States and the administrative measures to prepare for accession. Agreements with 13 Member States are in force, by the government's own list and the Commission's count, but the negotiations with Italy and Greece are only proposed and no outcome is recorded; these statuses are proposals. Adopting further agreements would not by itself close the gap.

Concluding agreements is in the key recommendation in the 2021 to 2025 reports, and social security coordination is a main strand of the chapter. The Commission's good preparation rating lowers the urgency but not the repeated requirement, so reviewers may reasonably weigh centrality differently.
Progress depends on other states agreeing, not only on the government. No new agreement is recorded from 2021 to 2025, including after the negotiations started in 2023.

The chapter scale was context only, and the 2025 ratings have nothing earlier to compare with. The recommendation on administrative measures recurs from 2020 to 2025, and the shift from identifying measures to putting them in place reflects wording, not a reported step.

What remains is removing citizenship conditions from the pension and health insurance laws, aligning with the regulations and putting administrative measures in place by accession. The Commission finds the framework partly aligned, but the plan to amend the legislation is only proposed within five years (a status that is itself a proposal).

Administrative measures for coordination are in the key recommendation in each report from 2020 to 2025, and alignment with the regulations is central to this strand of the chapter. The screening report requires alignment, including on nationality conditions, by accession.

The named legal changes are within national control, and the register law adopted in 2023 shows some related legislative activity. However, it spans the pension and health systems, needs prior analysis and has a plan of up to five years.

The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in the 2025 screening report, and the annual key recommendation adds electronic exchange only in 2025. The word 'still' suggests the issue is not new, so I do not call it new, and a single year cannot show a trend.

What remains is the human and IT capacity to exchange social security data through EESSI and to process EHIC data electronically. The registry and the EESSI preparations are only proposed (statuses that are themselves proposals), and the country reports no EHIC reader in its healthcare facilities.

Electronic exchange is central to applying coordination at accession, and the Commission asks for stepped-up effort. The support is thin, however, as it comes from the screening report and one annual key recommendation.

The planned registry has a stated World Bank loan and two-year horizon, but it rests on the country's own account. Several institutions are involved, EESSI access points follow later analysis over five years, and connection also involves the EU side, with no past progress recorded.

The chapter scale was context only. Nine agreements or nine Member States are recorded in each report from 2020 to 2024, and no development in 2024 and 2025. The 14 Member States in the 2025 report is a noted difference of scope, not growth, because the five added have agreements that do not include EHIC.

What remains is access through EHIC for citizens of the other Member States. Use with nine Member States is proposed as in practice (a status that is itself a proposal), and the Commission finds technical alignment satisfactory, but the card's use rests on separate arrangements and not on general entitlement.

This is a repeated finding across six reports, but the EHIC is not named in the key recommendation, which refers only to healthcare insurance agreements. The Commission treats technical alignment as satisfactory and it overlaps with RI-FMW-008.

The sources describe the basis differently: the country says unilateral use and the Commission says bilateral agreements, which matters because the first would be within national control and the second depends on others. The country reports that agreements could soon be reached with three more states, but no new agreement or development has been recorded.
All items come from one report, the 2025 screening report, so there is no sequence to read and the chapter scale cannot help.

What remains is alignment with Directives 98/49/EC and 2014/50/EU, apart from cross-border membership and equal treatment in voluntary funds. Those two exceptions are provided in law but enter into force only at accession, and no responding intervention is linked, so adoption does not count as closure.

The requirement is raised only in the screening report and in no key recommendation, and supplementary pensions are peripheral to the chapter compared with its main strands. It remains a stated acquis gap, so Low does not mean it can wait past accession.

Legal alignment is within national control and part of the framework is already drafted into law. However, the responsible unit is reported to have only one person and the Commission calls for thorough training.

The sub-area rating 'still at an early stage' matches this issue but appears only in 2025, so it is used with the issue's own items. The integrity policy is outstanding in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the framework is called weak in 2024 and again in the screening report.

What remains is a signed integrity policy, a person to implement it, a reinforced internal audit department and controls in the institutions concerned. No responding intervention is linked, so there is no status to compare, and the country's stated plan to sign has not been shown to be carried out.

The requirement is repeated by the Commission in three reports, but it is not in a key recommendation for the chapter or central to it. The issue's scope is limited to free movement of workers, and general anti-corruption policy is outside it.

Signing the policy and naming a person are small steps for one agency, but no report shows them done, though the agency reportedly planned to do so. Reinforcing audit staff, ministry capacity and controls across institutions is wider.

The evidence is from international organisations, with one research study, and partly regional, and no measure of this issue repeats over time for the country. The doubling of permits is regional and cannot alone support a finding here, and the Commission's permit counts have unclear bases. The chapter scale was not decisive, as it concerns EU workers' access.

No EU requirement item exists for this issue, so the comparison the gap requires cannot be made and no responding intervention is linked. The international organisations report, for North Macedonia, regulatory barriers, passport retention, wage deductions, underreporting and overlapping laws, which is what remains on their account; other items are regional. A regional claim that laws are EU-aligned does not name the country and sits uneasily with the Commission's finding of partial alignment for EU workers.

The issue is mainly raised by others: the evidence is from international organisations and partly regional, with no Commission recommendation on third-country workers in Chapter 2. The labour shortage it describes may matter for the country, but that is not the test for importance to accession.

The rules and inspection are national matters, without dependence on the EU, but the international organisation evidence, partly regional, points to several institutions, under-resourced inspection and permits tied to one employer. No item shows past progress for the country, so this is a provisional view.

The Commission states that the 2019 amendments further simplified the single application, which is not government reporting alone, though no processing data supports it. The World Bank in 2024 still reports regulatory barriers and asks for simpler permits, and quotas are reported regionally to add delay, so the wider result is less clear.
The Commission directly ties the simplification to the amendments, but this is one statement in one report, with no before and after measure.

The Commission itself rates preparation on coordination as good and gives the experience of the agreements as the reason, so this is not government reporting alone. The result is narrow: it concerns readiness, and the same report still finds the law only partly aligned.
The Commission states the causal link directly, but 'including through' shows that it does not treat the agreements as the only source of this experience. No independent test of the link exists.

The Commission finds technical alignment satisfactory and says the agreements allow EHIC use, but only nine Member States are covered and the country reports that data cannot be processed electronically. The Commission asks for stepped-up capacity to be ready at accession.

The Commission says bilateral agreements allow the use, and the country lists agreements that include EHIC with nine Member States. However, the country also says use is on a unilateral basis, so the mechanism is not settled.

The EU requirement first appears in 2025 (AI Act alignment and enforcement structures) and the only later EU item, in 2026, concerns the AI Factory Antenna, so there is no repeated EU wording to compare; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Separately, national sources show the gap is older than the EU ask: a 2024 government plan mentions AI as a future need, and the 2025 audit traces a stalled strategy to a 2021 working group, but these are one-year snapshots rather than a trend. The value therefore means new as an EU requirement, not new as a national gap.

Against the single EU alignment ask of 2025, the responding AI legislation and AI strategy are still proposed, and the adopted ICT strategy and signed Antenna grant do not supply alignment or enforcement; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is alignment with the AI Act and the enforcement structures it needs, none of which yet exists. National sources confirm the absence (machine-translated audit, capped at Medium), and the audit's statement that data protection law is aligned with the GDPR conflicts with the Commission's statement that full alignment is pending, which is left unresolved.

The rating rests only on the EU layer: one body-text invitation in the 2025 report to align fully with the AI Act, plus a 2026 readout that encourages outreach and does not mention the Act. It is not a benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, is absent from the 2025 Chapter 10 key recommendations and is not repeated, so it cannot be High; Medium reflects a requirement central to the AI theme with thin support. The much larger national audit, strategy and research evidence (over 200 of 229 items, mostly from a few documents) describes the gap but was given no weight here.

Drafting is within government control, with the EU Act as a template and AI legislation already listed in an adopted action plan, but enforcement structures need a designated authority, specialist staff and funding, across several bodies. The record is weak: one working group meeting since 2021, a digital assistant no longer functioning and no line of accountability between the ministry and the innovation fund, though a data protection law gives some base and an EU-funded Antenna grant is signed. This leans on machine-translated national evidence (capped at Medium), and the audit's finding that no public sector project has been implemented sits against its report of the Buki platform at a state university, a difference of scope it does not explain.

The only movement is that the key recommendation to finalise and adopt the ICT strategy, unchanged from 2020 to 2024, ended in 2025 because the strategy was adopted, and adoption is not improvement in governance. The Commission's wording that the ministry needs stronger capacity is unchanged across 2022 to 2025, which sets the default to persistent, and the 2025 report adds a call for more IT staff. The chapter scale (some progress 2020, limited 2021 to 2024, some 2025) is context only and was not decisive.

The latest EU items report the strategy adopted but still ask for stronger ministry capacity, more IT staff and the digital agency, which remains proposed and which the country has said it will reassess; these statuses are themselves proposals, and that of the National Council is unclear because the 2024 audit found no 2023 activity while the strategy cites its formation. What remains is applying the strategy, building coordinating capacity and IT staffing, and settling the agency question. The Commission's well-structured set-up and the national vacuum are a noted difference of scope, not a conflict.

The ICT strategy was a Chapter 10 key recommendation in five successive reports, and the ministry capacity ask has recurred in four reports to 2025, on an issue central to the digital transformation theme. The key recommendation itself left the list after adoption in 2025 and the capacity ask sits in body text, so High rests on treating adoption as the start rather than the end of the requirement. National plans and audits were not counted towards this rating.

A new ministry and an adopted strategy show that institutional steps can be taken, but the strategy took over five years and coordination depends on many institutions that have offered limited cooperation. IT posts are about half filled and public pay rules limit competition with the private sector, which the ministry cannot change alone. The staffing and working group evidence is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The change since the Commission's 2023 call for basic systems is the adoption of the electronic archiving law in 2025 and the Reform Agenda steps themselves, and adoption alone does not show improvement. The Commission's technical checks found the document system only partially operational, and use has barely moved, from 21 institutions in 2022 to 22 in 2025, on machine-translated national figures capped at Medium. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive.

Of the three Reform Agenda requirements, the law is adopted and the Commission treats that step as achieved, but it applied only from June 2026 with by-laws still proposed, the e-platform is proposed and the document system is only partially operational; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is application of the law, the storage and record-keeping platform, the single document system across all central institutions and the digital mailbox. No item in the input shows whether the 2026 deadlines were met.

The archiving law, the storage platform and the single document system are named Reform Agenda steps with payments attached, and these shared systems are central to the digital government theme. The rating rests on those EU conditions, not on the many national plan items.

The tasks are bounded, led by one ministry and backed by payment incentives, and the legal step was achieved by its 2025 deadline. Roll-out is harder: it needs hardware, licences, training and change of working habits in many institutions, and earlier piloting left 22 institutions using a small part of the system. The national evidence on use is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The Commission's wording is close to unchanged across reports: advancing but low in 2020 to 2023, advancing slowly in 2024 and 2025, and low in 2026, with one 2025 note that SME adoption has accelerated but stays uneven and basic. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 54.5% website figure repeats across reports and was not treated as new evidence, and the 3% and 19.7% online sales figures use different populations, so they show no trend.

The latest EU asks concern support to companies through the innovation hub and active use of Digital Europe calls; the hub is set up and the association agreement signed, while vouchers, the support portal and the grant mechanism are proposed, and these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is actual use of these channels and SME adoption beyond basic technologies, as the Commission still reported low digitalisation in 2026.

The finding is repeated in most years, largely in economic governance documents, but it has few specific recommendations; the only key recommendation found is the 2025 hub item, and no benchmark or payment condition names it in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU concern that is not central to accession steps.

Government can fund and steer support, and EU programmes and a first hub already exist, but results depend on many small firms' demand, skills and finance. Past effort is small and not evaluated: EUR 0.5 million budgeted in 2023, and the strategy itself says there has been no support mechanism for projects of greater national importance; that source is machine translated and capped at Medium.

The ask to align with the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act recurs with little change in the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and e-commerce was described as slow in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. Growth figures for online transactions are country-reported, partly repeated and on differing bases, so they were not read as closing the issue.

The latest EU items still require alignment with the DSA, DMA and Geo-blocking Regulation, and the responding alignment measures are all proposed, with national targets of 2027 and 2028 and only training delivered; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is the alignment itself for all these acts, plus full alignment on electronic commerce. The country's report of being largely aligned with the e-Commerce Directive and the Commission's call to align fully differ in degree and speaker, and were not treated as closure.

The requirement is repeated in three reports and relates to binding acquis, but it sits in Chapter 10 body text, not in the 2024 or 2025 key recommendations, and is not named as a benchmark or payment condition in the input. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central under the criteria.

The work is mainly legislative with EU texts as templates, a government timetable and a request for expert group participation, which depends partly on the Commission. No draft is reported and past progress is limited to training, and applying platform rules will need capacity that the input does not evidence.

The alignment ask on digital tools in company law recurs in near-identical wording in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, so the default applies; the chapter scale is context only and was not decisive. The 2025 screening finding of a high level of alignment shows the remaining ask is narrow, but it is not evidence of change over time.

Fully online company registration is in practice and the Commission finds high alignment, on a status that is itself a proposal. What remains is further alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151, including scrutiny of a company's object and verification of directors' appointment and disqualification. The country's statement that it is aligned and the Commission's statement that further alignment is necessary are a confirmed contradiction, reported here and not resolved.

It appears in the key recommendations of three reports, but always bundled with other company law items, and digital tools are a narrow strand on which the Commission already finds high alignment. It is therefore a repeated EU requirement that is not central to the chapter, and it is not a benchmark or payment condition in the input.

The remaining points are specific legal amendments in a field with few actors and a working one-stop-shop registry, and they depend on no other institution's roll-out. The ask has nonetheless stood since 2021 with no reported draft, which is why the rating depends on the small scope and not on past momentum.

The only evidence for this positive result is one general statement by the State Audit Office, in the government family and machine translated, with no measured change in response times. The same report says full implementation did not succeed, so success is not judged. The State Audit Office is treated as independent, as validated at G2.
No measured outcome exists to attribute to the pilot. The audit's sentence describes what the pilot suggests AI can do, not an observed effect.

The audit says full implementation did not succeed because more money was requested for training, although the pilot itself ran. The only direct evidence is the machine-translated State Audit Office report, capped at Medium; it sits in the government family, but is rated independent of the executive in source quality, so the reviewers should decide whether it counts as government reporting. The State Audit Office is treated as independent, as validated at G2.
The audit states a direct cause, a funding request for further training, but this is one machine-translated source and no other source tests it.

The 2021 working group met once and produced no strategy, the 2025 action plan still lists drafting one, and a non-government paper describes slow progress, though it draws partly on the same audit. The only direct evidence is the machine-translated State Audit Office report, capped at Medium; it sits in the government family, but is rated independent of the executive in source quality, so the reviewers should decide whether it counts as government reporting. Failure here covers this route to date and not the later measure, which remains proposed. The State Audit Office is treated as independent, as validated at G2.
The non-delivery is directly tied to the working group's inactivity, but the audit does not explain why it stopped and other causes cannot be excluded. The audit is machine translated.

The audit says the assistant launched in April 2023 is not functioning two years later after about EUR 150 thousand was spent; a research paper repeats this but relies on the audit, so it is not independent support. The only direct evidence is the machine-translated State Audit Office report, capped at Medium; it sits in the government family, but is rated independent of the executive in source quality, so the reviewers should decide whether it counts as government reporting. The State Audit Office is treated as independent, as validated at G2.
The outcome is the state of the tool itself, so the link is direct, but the audit gives no reason for the failure and it rests on one machine-translated source.

The Commission says adoption facilitates the use of e-government tools, but its report predates the law's application from 1 June 2026, by-laws were still to come, and no later item shows use. Adoption is not success.
The Commission's sentence asserts an expected effect, and no observed change in use is available to attribute to a law that was not yet applicable.

The Commission's recommendation to keep extending taxpayer e-services recurs every year from 2020 to 2026 with almost no change, moving only from 'further extend' to 'continue the process of expansion', so the default applies; this is one repeated view, not independent evidence. The Chapter 16 'Some progress' wording of 2021 is context only and was not decisive.

The Commission still asks in 2026 for expansion, while e-Tax, e-VAT and pre-filled returns are proposed as in practice and the electronic tax administration only as proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the Macedonian-language plan items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. What remains is a wider range of taxpayer e-services, with the electronic tax administration still at project documentation and draft legislation stage.

The recommendation is repeated across more than three reports, but taxpayer e-services are one clause beside business processes, the integrated IT system and compliance risk, so the issue is not central to Chapter 16 or the theme. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the fiscal sector only as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.

One agency leads, working platforms exist, and upgrades are reported by the Commission, so progress depends little on other actors or the EU. A caution is that the source does not say how far further e-services depend on the integrated IT system, which has been outstanding since 2020.
The Commission states that e-Tax is a successful e-service that has simplified tax reporting, and its 2021 report on reduced burden points the same way, but no measure of the simplification is given.
The Commission names e-Tax directly as the cause of simpler reporting, which is plausible given the system's function. The claim is general and unmeasured, so confidence stops at Medium.
The Commission lists e-VAT among successful e-services, but the outcome stated is only that it enables VAT returns, which is availability and not a result. No figures on use are given.
No result beyond the function of the application is stated, so there is nothing to attribute.
The 2023 sentence repeats the 2022 wording on e-Tax, so it is not independent support for LNK-000432 and the same limits apply: a Commission statement with no measure.
As for LNK-000432: the Commission names the system directly, the claim is unmeasured, and the repeated wording adds no independent weight.
The 2023 wording repeats 2022 and states only that e-VAT makes online returns possible, which is availability and not a result. No figures on use are given.
No result beyond the function of the application is stated, so there is nothing to attribute.

The e-market moved from development in 2021 to launch in 2022, and awards rose from 70 in 2022 to 258 in 2023 (259 in the Reform Agenda, a minor difference of count), with 350 small-value transactions in 2024, though that item does not name the e-market. The Commission's finding of poor use in 2023 is not repeated later, and no later item shows change on e-catalogues or red-flag analysis. The Chapter 5 'Limited progress' wording of 2022 and 2025 is context only and was not decisive.

The system is working and the e-market and red-flag modules are proposed as in practice, with the low-value bylaw at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is raising e-market use from 350 to the required 800 awards in 2026, wider take-up of e-catalogues, and the data analysis the Commission asked for in 2023.

E-market use is a Reform Agenda payment condition, which meets one limb of the High test, but the Commission finds the core system functions efficiently and the shortfall concerns low-value contracts and add-on modules. It is therefore not central to Chapter 5 or the theme, and the proposal rests on that reading of centrality.

One bureau runs a platform that is already obligatory for all contracting authorities, awards rose about fivefold in two years, and a payment is attached to the target. The main limit is the confidence of contracting authorities, and the target is still more than double the 2024 count.

The Commission states that red flags contributed to enhanced administrative control by the Bureau. It is one qualitative statement with no measure, and the Commission still asked in 2023 for the system to be developed further.
The Commission's wording is 'contributed to', stated in the same sentence as the portal upgrade, and no data separate the two.

The Commission assessment states that the system significantly benefited from e-appeals, and the country's description of the function fits, though it alone would not show success. The conflict on timing (still being developed in 2020; reported as fully operational from April 2019) does not affect the 2023 assessment but is unresolved.
The Commission names e-appeals directly, but 'benefited' is general and no measure of the benefit is given.

The Commission assessment states that e-appeals provided an efficient and transparent system for submitting and conducting appeals. This comes from the same passage as LNK-000437 and is not independent of it, and no figures are given.

The outcome is the working of the appeals function itself, so there is little room for another cause. This concerns the link only; the strength of the outcome still rests on one unmeasured Commission statement.

The Commission assessment states that a high level of transparency was achieved through the electronic procurement and e-appeals system, which is a finding on transparency only. It does not say that corruption fell.
The Commission credits e-appeals jointly with the wider electronic system, and the source does not separate their shares.

The same Commission sentence as LNK-000439 credits the electronic system with a high level of transparency, and it says nothing on whether corruption fell. Its obligatory coverage is reported by the country and supports the claim only as description.
The Commission credits the electronic system jointly with e-appeals, and transparency has other possible sources that the sentence does not address.

The requirement that the point of single contact be upgraded to meet the Services Directive is unchanged in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the register of regulated professions moves from unfinished data validation (2020, 2021) to 'yet to be put in place' (2024, 2025). The contact point itself did advance, from early stage in 2021 to a platform with 312 online services in 2025, so the two limbs of this issue point different ways. No Chapter 3 scale rating is linked to the issue, and the scale would be context only.

A contact point platform exists and is proposed as implemented, but the Commission finds it not fully in line with the acquis and the list and register still absent; these statuses are themselves proposals. Sources conflict on which body is the contact point (Central Register or uslugi.gov.mk), and the 238 (2023) and 124 (2024) service counts are not explained. What remains is full online information and procedures under the Services Directive, especially on licences, and a transparent electronic register of all regulated professions.

The point of single contact was a key recommendation only in 2021, 2022 and 2023, with the 2021 item flagged as doubtful for the theme, and later Commission items on it and the 2025 item on the register of professions are in body text, so the requirement is repeated. It is a sector portal under the Services Directive and is not central to the digital government theme, which is the same reading applied to taxpayer e-services (RI-TEC-005) and e-procurement (RI-TEC-006). Its importance to Chapter 3 is not the test for a technology issue, and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition names it.

The platform is in place and service numbers have been added, which favours progress on the contact point. Against that, sectoral laws must be aligned, the responsible body is unclear between sources, and a register of all professions needs input from many regulators.

The claim that the new Central Register portal simplified procedures comes only from the country presentation, and government reporting alone cannot show success. The Commission reports one-day online registration without naming this portal, and also finds simplification underexploited for business registration, so independent evidence does not settle it.
Only the country's own statement connects the portal to simpler procedures, so no independent basis for attribution exists.

Commission wording on extending Moj Termin is the same in 2022 and 2023, and non-interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data recurs in 2024 and 2025, with non-alignment of legislation added in the 2025 screening. Functional upgrades in 2023 and 2025 are real but have not changed the stated shortfall. The default for three unchanged reports is not strictly triggered, and no Chapter 28 scale rating was decisive.

The 2025 report still asks for interoperability, and the responding steps are proposed (population register and wallet connections) or at insufficient evidence (platform for traceability), none naming Health Insurance Fund data; these statuses are themselves proposals and the plan items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The paper-referral finding and the screening's account of a tool holding referrals are a noted difference, not a conflict, since storing data and issuing on paper can both be true, but practice needs checking. What remains is interoperability with Health Insurance Fund data, an end to paper referrals, and alignment with the eHealth acquis.

The Commission's requirement is repeated in 2024 and 2025 and raised to a recommendation in 2025, but it is a narrow part of Chapter 28 and only recently prominent. The Reform Agenda's e-services step names the health sector as an example, and this was not read as a payment condition on this issue.

A central tool and one lead ministry exist and upgrades are reported, but interoperability needs the Health Insurance Fund as well, and alignment with the acquis needs legislation. National plan and World Bank items add that the platform needs upgrading and users need digital literacy; the plan item is machine translated, capped at Medium confidence.

ITU states that Moj Termin improved patient management, but that item is flagged as a possible misread. Later sources point to limits: the World Bank says the system could be updated to improve efficiency, and the Commission finds that referrals remain on paper and the system is not interoperable.
ITU names the system directly, but the claim is general and unmeasured, its item has Medium confidence with a possible misread flag, and patient management has other possible drivers.

The Commission states that Moj Termin helped to significantly reduce waiting times, while recommending extension to primary care doctors. No figures are given, and later criticism concerns appointment-system quality and interoperability, not this past effect.
The wording 'helped to' is a stated contribution, not sole cause, and no measurement or comparison is given.
The 2023 sentence repeats the 2022 wording, so it is not independent support for LNK-000442 and the same limits apply: a Commission statement with no figures.
As for LNK-000442: 'helped to' states a contribution, there is no measurement, and the repeated wording adds no independent weight.

Commission calls for digital court communication and connected IT recur in 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025, with identical wording in the last two, and the single 2026 item on the administrative courts cannot alone show a change of direction. Support is thin (eight items, none for 2021 or 2022, most flagged theme_doubtful), and no chapter scale was decisive.

The administrative courts' interconnection is proposed as implemented and the Commission calls it a key advancement, but no status is recorded for the judicial IT strategies and council, and Luris is at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals. What remains is digital communication with courts generally, videoconferencing for hearings, and connections between other justice institutions, including the Ministry of Justice and the prosecution.

The recommendation is repeated, including in the 2024 and 2025 reports, within the important Chapter 23 area, but digital communication is a supporting part of judicial reform and no benchmark or payment condition on it appears in the input. Evidence is thin and most items are flagged theme_doubtful.

One interconnection shows that progress is possible, but several independent justice institutions must act together, and the Commission points to weak coordination. The evidence on actors and resources is thin, so this rating is tentative.

From 2020 to 2026 the Commission repeats the same shortfall: too few fully transactional services, low use and below-expectation results, ending with 'quite underdeveloped' in 2026, and the world index rank falls from 72 to 80 to 84 (the last from a machine-translated strategy table, capped at Medium confidence). The 2025 report does record a real change, with most-demanded services and some certificates now online, so the case for 'improving' is open but rests on one report that the 2026 finding does not bear out. The Chapter 10 scale (Some, Limited, Limited, Some progress in 2020, 2023, 2024, 2025) is context only and was not decisive, and service counts were not used for trend because their definitions differ.

The portal is proposed as in practice and its upgrade as implemented, while the Reform Agenda reform is proposed; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the upgrade status sits uneasily with the Commission's 2024 note that the 135 services were not yet configured. Progress against the 50% target cannot be fixed, because the 264 baseline conflicts with the Commission's 392 and 124 figures, and 246 also conflicts with 124, so sources are cited both ways. What remains is a much wider set of fully transactional, commonly requested services that people actually use, on an agreed count, and equal access, where the Commission's statement that the portal caters for special needs conflicts with the audit's finding (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.

The e-services increase is a Reform Agenda payment condition, and widening the portal's services is a recommendation repeated across three or more reports, including 'treat as a priority' in the 2025 screening. It is central to the digital government theme and Chapter 10. The rating rests on these, not on the large number of national audit and strategy items.

A single platform, EU funding and a dated payment step favour progress, and the Commission reports new services in 2025. Against that, the Commission's own wording shows the 135-service upgrade slipping for years and fragmented ownership, and the State Audit Office (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) reports about 140 laws unaligned and 101 of 242 posts unfilled, which means many institutions must act.

No repeated Commission wording or comparable series exists: EU items are isolated additions (2024, 2025), and the Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive. The other signals are partial and mixed, since e-Rabota's share of employer registrations rose from 60% to 69% but fell from 67% to 62% for agencies in government reports, and a civil society study finds general slow progress at municipal level. Government and civil society items here are Low or Medium confidence, and the Macedonian ones are machine translated.

Sector services exist, and One Stop Shops are proposed as implemented, while the analysis on e-services there, the mobile offices and the employment plan are proposed or at insufficient evidence; these statuses are themselves proposals, and the national items are machine translated, capped at Medium confidence. The Commission's requirement is general, not specific. What remains is a wider range and use of sector and local services, including municipal ones, with published statistics on delivery.

The Commission mentions sector services only briefly, and most of the concern is raised by the national audit (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence), national plans and civil society, so the issue meets the test of being mainly raised by others. The Reform Agenda target falls on the national portal under the G5 split, and item volume was not counted.

Individual sector bodies can and do make progress, as e-Rabota and the Cadastre Office show. Across many institutions and municipalities, however, the audit and ICT strategy (machine translated, capped at Medium confidence) describe parallel systems built without clear guidance, and no single actor has control.
The Commission reports measured results: unresolved cases down 20% compared with 2024 and the backlog down 10%. This is one period only, and the figures' origin is not stated in the sentence.
The Commission's wording links the new digital services directly to the fall, but other changes at the Cadastre Office are not ruled out and there is no comparison.

Commission wording that the law needs further alignment repeated from 2020 to 2022, and the matching sub-area wording in 2023 was no progress, but the wording then changed: the 2025 assessment found significant gaps after the new law, and the 2026 assessment found alignment partially achieved after the December 2025 amendments. The chapter-wide limited progress of 2024 is context only and was not decisive. Sources conflict on the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive: the Commission said in 2024 that the country was yet to align, while the country's reported view in the screening is full alignment, and this is not resolved here.

The Commission's May 2026 assessment considers the Reform Agenda step not achieved and the beneficiary considers it achieved, as it did in 2025, so the two sides conflict and the Commission's finding is the requirement compared here. Responding interventions carry proposed statuses that the reviewers check at G6: the 2025 law and December amendments adopted, the by-laws and 2026 draft amendments only proposed, and the law applicable only from 1 June 2026, with no evidence on the outcome of the grace period ending 30 June 2026. What remains is closing the harmonisation gaps with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act in both laws and adopting and applying the by-laws; the ePrivacy conflict is left to its own issue under the taxonomy.

Adoption of an aligned law is a Reform Agenda step with a payment provision, and alignment with the Code recurs in the Commission's chapter recommendations from 2022 to 2025. It is central to the digital infrastructure theme because other reforms in the area rest on this legal framework. The roaming and net neutrality parts of the issue are largely positive and do not drive this rating.

The mechanisms are legal alignment and implementing rules, led by one ministry with the regulator and parliament, and a new law and amendments were adopted in 2025, which favours progress. Against that, the Commission assessed the Reform Agenda step as not achieved in both 2025 and 2026, with gaps remaining in two laws, and the by-laws are described as technically demanding and were not yet due. Adoption has been quick but alignment has twice fallen short, which does not support High.

Commission concern about the regulator's independence recurs in nearly unchanged terms in each report from 2020 to 2025, with no recorded improvement, so the default applies; in September 2024 parliament dismissed all five commission members, which the source reports without saying what it meant for independence. The chapter scale was not decisive. The competition part has moved a little, from no relevant developments in 2020 and 2021 to a market still shared by two operators in 2023 and a new operator taking part in a frequency tender in 2025, so the two parts of this issue do not move together.

The latest Commission items still ask for the regulator's independence to be ensured and bolstered, and the 2025 law's statement that the Agency is independent is a legal provision, not evidence of practice. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the law is adopted, while the third operator and the frequency tender are only proposed, and the latest evidence on the tender is a sole bidder with a decision deadline of 12 January 2026, in machine-translated regulator reporting. What remains is independence shown in appointments and practice, more competition in a concentrated mobile market, and resolving the financing provisions for the Operational and Technical Agency, on which the Commission and the country disagree and which concern that agency and not the regulator itself.

Strengthening the independence and capacity of this regulator is a key Commission recommendation repeated in every report from 2021 to 2025, and an independent regulator is central to the digital infrastructure theme. It is not itself a Reform Agenda step, and the recommendation is shared with the media regulators, which are outside this issue. The rating rests on the independence part; the competition part is supported by repeated but less prominent findings.

The two parts differ. Independence looks hard, because it depends on appointments by parliament and exposure to political interests, and six years of reports record no progress, while competition looks more realistic because a tender has reached a compliant bid. That tender rests on one bidder and was held up by elections and a missing opinion from the anti-corruption commission, as machine-translated regulator reporting states, so Medium is a blend that would not hold if the issue were split.

The Commission's sentence that smaller companies still face obstacles repeats from 2021 to 2026 with the same figures, so the default applies, though repeats are not independent evidence, and in 2025 the wording hardened to significant obstacles for smaller companies and rural areas. National averages did rise, with home internet access at 90.8% in 2024, 5G coverage at 76% in 2023 and 97% in a machine-translated 2025 national source, and some progress on ICT infrastructure in matching sub-area wording in 2025, while differences between earlier household figures reflect different measures, not conflict. No series tracks the rural and small-business gap itself, so the averages do not show that the unevenness has narrowed, and the chapter scale was not decisive.

Latest EU items still ask for more access for smaller companies and rural areas, while the compared statuses, which are proposals for G6, show 5G roll-out in practice but the national optical network only proposed. Sources conflict on the size of the gap: the ICT strategy gives 77% fixed coverage against an EU average of 78%, the Commission gives 79.6% against 93.1%, and the strategy elsewhere gives 77% as very high capacity coverage after stating 69%, so the comparison with the EU cannot be relied on until the measures are checked. What remains is fixed broadband for small firms and rural areas, very low take-up of the fastest connections, and completing the 5G roll-out named in the Reform Agenda.

Roll-out of 5G network and services is named in a Reform Agenda step, and the Commission repeats the particular need to increase access to broadband in its assessments from 2021 to 2026, which makes it central to the digital infrastructure theme. The payment condition covers the 5G part, not the rural and small-business part, which appears in repeated assessments and not in the chapter's key recommendations. The large volume of items on this issue, much of it repeated wording and national statistics, did not raise the rating.

Past progress is clear on 5G and on general access, where operators have invested and the Commission records continued expansion. The harder part depends on resources and on others: rural and low-demand areas lack commercial interest, the national network is at feasibility stage on a timetable to 2030 with mixed financing, and the government's own strategy, in machine translation, names lack of finance and high prices as challenges. Delivery therefore needs the ministry, the public broadcasting enterprise, operators and outside funders.

The plan's implementation slowed in 2021 and was further delayed in 2022, a strategic approach to broadband was found lacking in 2022 and 2023, the plan was said only to remain valid in 2024 and 2025, and the 2025 screening asks for its targets to be aligned with the Digital Decade; the 2020 chapter-wide some progress is context and was not decisive. Newer Reform Agenda investment and a feasibility study are plans and do not yet show change, so this is not improving, and no 2026 Commission item addresses the framework. Sources conflict on the plan's period, with ITU and the 2025 report giving 2019-2029 and the 2022 and 2024 reports giving 2019-2023, which affects how far the delays can be measured against targets.

The latest EU items ask for targets aligned with the Digital Decade, further alignment on aid for broadband and stronger capacity at the public broadcasting enterprise. The compared statuses are proposals for G6: the ICT strategy with its 2030 goals is adopted, but its alignment with the Digital Decade is the government's own statement in machine translation, and target alignment, State aid and the national network are only proposed, while none of the three plan measures towards the 100 Mbps target has been implemented. What remains is updating the plan's targets, settling the aid rules and financing the backhaul network; the reported non-use of the Western Balkans Investment Framework for infrastructure sits beside technical assistance from it for a feasibility study, which appears to be a difference between study and construction but should be checked.

The requirement is repeated by the EU, in the 2022 and 2023 assessments and the 2025 screening, but it is not named in a benchmark, a Reform Agenda payment step or the chapter's key recommendations. The Reform Agenda plan does call the broadband network the most important digital project, but as an investment, so the issue matters for the theme with thinner support than the legal and regulator issues.

Updating targets is within the government's control and a mapping study is the stated first step, but financing the network depends on outside funders, State aid alignment and a public enterprise whose capacity the Commission says needs strengthening. Past progress is weak: the plan was delayed in 2021 and 2022, and the national broadband competence office, reported in machine translation, finds none of three measures implemented. The financing figures come from a table flagged as possibly misread, so they support only the general point that funding is mixed.

The Commission's country report states that the public benefited from decreased roaming prices, and later Commission reports record the roaming-free zone in the country. No price series is in the evidence, so the finding rests on Commission statements.
The source says the lower prices resulted from the agreement, and a binding regional agreement is a plausible direct cause. Without price data, other influences on prices cannot be excluded.

The reduction is stated in a regional Commission communication that does not name the country, so it relies on the country report for the finding about North Macedonia. The dates differ only because they are phases of one agreement, not a conflict.
The source states the agreement led to the reductions, and the schedule fits a direct effect. No price series confirms the size or timing in the country.

The regional communication reports the elimination of charges under roam like at home, and the country report confirms citizens benefit from the roaming-free zone since 1 July 2021. The regulator's report dates the regime to 1 June 2021 in Low confidence machine translation, and this date conflict is noted but does not change the result.
Abolishing these charges was the direct purpose of the agreement and the regime exists because of it. The sources describe no competing cause.

The Commission's country report states that the agreement was fully implemented and that the country has benefited from the roaming-free zone since July 2021. This is Commission evidence, not government reporting.
The zone is the direct result of implementing the agreement, and the same report links the two. The sources describe no competing cause.

The regional communication states that the agreement brought about roam like at home from 1 July 2021, and the country report confirms this for North Macedonia. The Commission is here describing a process it helped to secure, so the source is not fully detached.

The scheme was created by this agreement, so the causal link is direct. The credit the source gives to the Commission and the Regional Cooperation Council concerns securing the agreement, not a separate cause of the scheme.
This repeats the 2022 statement in nearly the same words, so it is not independent new evidence for the result. The finding about the country again relies on the country report.
The scheme was introduced by this agreement, as with the earlier statement, and the sources describe no competing cause.

The outcome item is the country's reported view in the screening report, which alone would not support a result. The result rests on the Commission's own 2022 country report, not on this view or on the authorities' report of no consumer complaints.
The regime was introduced under this agreement, and the Commission's own account agrees with the reported view on this point.

The Commission reports a first phased reduction from October 2023, but the aim is near-domestic prices by 2027 in the roadmap and by 2028 in the operators' glide path, which differ as ambition and commercial schedule. The items are regional and none shows the effect on prices in North Macedonia, and agreements to extend the zone were still being prepared in 2025.

The Commission reports the first phased reduction directly after the roadmap's adoption but does not say the roadmap caused it. The earlier reports place voluntary operator negotiations within the same process, and the reduction itself came from those operators, so the link is one of sequence and shared process only.

The first reduction came into force on 1 October 2023 and further steps run towards 2028, so only the opening stage can be seen. The items are regional and do not name the country, so they cannot alone support a finding about North Macedonia.
The outcome is close to being the agreement taking effect, so the link is nearly circular at regional level. Which operators and prices in North Macedonia were affected is not shown.

The Commission reports the 5G signal expanded to Skopje in line with the plan's targets, which shows network roll-out and not use or effect, and the coverage figures held do not fill that gap. It says in line with and states no cause, while also reporting the plan as slowed and delayed and operators as investing, so the outcome cannot be scored as a result of the plan.
The source says in line with the targets and states no cause. Roll-out depended on frequencies granted by the regulator and on operators' investment, which may have happened without the plan.

The sole bid and the extended deadline of 12 January 2026 come only from machine-translated regulator reporting, and the Commission confirms only that a new operator took part in a tender. No item shows an award or any effect on competition, so no result can be judged from the evidence held.

The bid plainly arose from the tender, but that says nothing about the intended result of more competition, and the only evidence of the bid's detail is government reporting. Attribution cannot be judged before an award is evidenced.

The Commission repeated the need to improve population register data in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and the same recommendation to complete the digitalisation of institutions' registers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, with use of the register still limited in 2024. The 2025 mention of efforts does not change the recommendation, so the default of persistent applies. The Chapter 10 scale is context only and was not decisive.

The population register is proposed as in practice, but the register platform, the Register of Registers and the wider e-services reform are all proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is to complete the digitalisation of institutional, municipal property and intellectual property registers and to raise the quality and use of population register data. The fully digital National Real Estate Register and the Commission's analogue property registers are a noted difference of register and level, not a conflict, and the machine-translated strategy on low use is capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission's main findings gave the same key recommendation to complete register digitalisation in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and base registers are central to the digital government theme. The recommendation is one clause of a wider one on administrative procedures and is shared with the data exchange and e-services issues, which reviewers may weigh. The Reform Agenda payment step on a register of charges is flagged as doubtful for this theme and was not relied on.

The operating population register shows that delivery is possible, and a register platform was begun with EU support. Against that, completion needs many institutions and municipalities to act, and the strategy's baseline of no digital registers in 2022 shows how much remains. The two strategy items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

Commission items ask for regular data updates in 2020 and more proactive disclosure in 2022, while amendments for Open Data Directive alignment were in preparation in 2023 and still with a working group in 2025; the 2020 sub-area rating of some progress concerns transparency more widely and, like the chapter scale, was not decisive. The State Audit Office reports that the portal has not functioned since early 2025, in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and the country's published screening presentation describes the portal favourably without addressing this. That outage rests on one source with no later status, so it does not yet support worsening, though confirmation would.

A Law on the Use of Public Sector Data is adopted and 580 datasets were reported by 2022, but the amendments and the Directive alignment action are proposed only, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is alignment with the Open Data Directive and regular publication by institutions on a functioning portal. Sources conflict, since the October 2025 strategy says the country is not aligned while the screening report's country presentation says partially aligned, so both are the country's own statements (the conflict register attributes the second to the Commission), and the Commission's own finding is only that further efforts are needed; the machine-translated items are capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission raises the matter in 2020, 2022 and 2025, but not in its main findings, so it is a repeated requirement that is not central. Most items here come from one national audit and one national strategy, and that volume was not treated as importance.

One ministry leads, the portal and 74 publishing institutions already existed by 2022, and the stated cause of the outage is a procurement problem rather than a structural one. Progress does not depend on the EU, although the amendments have been slow since 2023. This view leans on machine-translated items capped at Medium confidence, and government reporting on datasets does not itself show success.

The Commission found no concrete progress on the Law Enforcement Directive in 2020, partial alignment and a need for full alignment in 2023, and pending alignment in 2024 and 2025, so the requirement has not changed across three or more reports. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2024 and 2025 covers more than this issue and was not decisive. The 2025 transfer amendment without equivalent safeguards is a further concern but a single event.

The 2020 law is proposed as in practice, with the Commission confirming full application from August 2021, while the amendments and the Law Enforcement Directive law are proposed only, the earlier draft was withdrawn in 2022, and all these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is full alignment with the General Data Protection Regulation, a law transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, safeguards for transfers, harmonised sector laws and confirmed ePrivacy alignment. Sources conflict, since the State Audit Office and the Agency's strategy describe the law as aligned while the Commission calls the framework insufficient, and the country claims full ePrivacy alignment while the Commission seeks further efforts; this judgement does not rely on Article 122 of the unofficial translation (MKD-GOV-2020-001-0043), which may be mistranslated and, read literally, would suspend core chapters until accession.

Full alignment with the data protection rules is central to the data theme and is repeated by the Commission in 2023, 2024 and 2025, but none of the 2020 to 2025 reports names it in the key recommendations, and it is in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition. The 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress, but that is a finding and not a key recommendation, so this is a central requirement with thin support under the test. National and agency items were not counted.
override_reason: G6-D02: full alignment is core acquis, is repeated in 2023 to 2025, and the 2024 and 2025 main findings record no progress; the working test that lowered it was stricter than the judgement rules.

reason: Texts already exist: the Agency drafted amendments in April 2022 and a Law Enforcement Directive draft reached Parliament with, as the Agency reports, a positive informal Commission opinion. Yet the Government withdrew that draft in 2022, neither process moved in 2025, and sector laws need several ministries. The Agency's annual report items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission moved from dependence on ministries in 2021 and understaffing in 2022 and 2023 to staff falling further in 2024 and no director in 2025, with reported staff of 21, then 20, then 18 at the end of 2024 and 17 at the end of 2025. The last two counts are the Agency's own, machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, but they run the same way as the Commission's findings. The Agency reports a director from 5 December 2025, which is a later date than the Commission's finding, not a conflict, and the chapter scale was not decisive.

The amendments meant to secure the Agency's autonomy are proposed only, and the 2025-2030 strategy's proposed status of implemented means only that work has begun, with the Commission finding it was held back; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is autonomy in hiring and spending, and funding and staff that match the Agency's tasks. Statements that the Agency is independent describe its legal status, while the Commission and the Agency's own reports describe its operating dependence, so this is a noted difference and not a conflict.

The Commission has raised the Agency's dependence and capacity from 2021 to 2025 and an independent authority is central to the data theme, but the requirement appears only in body text, in 2023 and 2025 and in the 2025 communication in general terms. It is in no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition, and the main findings do not mention it, so it is a central requirement with thin support, on the same footing as RI-TEC-019.

Only a few domestic actors are needed, a draft has existed since April 2022 and the budget is small. Past progress is poor, however: the draft has not moved, the Ministry of Finance repeatedly refused funds or returned the employment plan, and the director post took most of 2025 to fill. The Agency's reports are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, and they are a party's account of its own constraints.

The Commission's finding was essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2024, with some progress noted in 2021, and then changed in 2025, when the Government removed the Agency from the mandatory consultation list and Parliament amended the law without consulting it. The sub-area rating of no progress in 2025 matches this issue and the chapter scale was not decisive. The Agency's report confirms the deletion in machine-translated text capped at Medium confidence, and its count of opinions (5 for 2024, 15 for 2025) does not show that consultation improved.

No intervention is recorded as responding to this issue, and the one recent measure, the removal from the consultation list, has a proposed status of implemented and runs the opposite way; these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is systematic consultation of the Agency on sector and implementing laws, follow-up of its recommendations and follow-up of its reports in Parliament.

The finding recurs in every report from 2020 to 2025 and the Commission called the 2025 removal concerning, but the 2023 list of areas requiring alignment does not include it and it is not in the main findings. It is a repeated requirement that supports the authority's role rather than being central to the theme, and reviewers may weigh the 2025 reversal differently.

Restoring the consultation duty is a change to the Government's own Rules of Procedure, which the Agency identifies precisely and which depends on no one outside the country. Getting ministries to follow advice and Parliament to act on reports is harder, and the Government removed the duty recently. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission called fines low in 2020, found in general that controllers do not implement the law in 2023, and in 2025 found low awareness and more frequent breaches, some unreported; the 2022 statement of progress on compliance sits in the paragraph on one body's supervision, so it is not a general trend. The Agency's statements of significant progress concern its own application of the framework, a noted difference from the Commission's sub-area rating, and supervision counts measure enforcement rather than compliance. The chapter scale was not decisive, and the machine-translated Agency findings are capped at Medium confidence.

The security rulebook has been adopted and the e-classroom is proposed as implemented, but the data protection officer network and the sanction amendments are proposed only, no independent evidence shows changed behaviour, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is for controllers, including public bodies, to apply the law, report breaches and face effective sanctions. Reprimand counts conflict between the Commission's report (10 for 2022, 17 for 2021) and the country presentation (4 for each), and low notification numbers (19 for 2022, 11 for 2025) are read by the Agency as under-reporting, so they do not conflict with the Commission's finding of more frequent breaches.

Compliance is central to whether the law has effect, but the Commission's direct findings on it are thin, mainly 2023 and 2025, and it is not a named key recommendation. The large volume of items comes from the Agency's own reports and was not treated as importance.

Progress needs behaviour to change across very many public and private controllers, and it depends on an Agency whose supervision and misdemeanour capacity is shrinking. The evidence shows awareness work and enforcement activity, but no sustained improvement in compliance. The Agency's items are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence.

The Commission used the same wording in three documents, its 2022 and 2023 reports and the 2023 screening report, but no item after 2023 addresses the issue, so the record shows neither that it continues nor that it has eased. The three-report default for persistent was therefore not applied, because the repeats span only two years and the 2024 and 2025 reports are silent. The chapter scale was not decisive.

The latest requirement, from 2023, is unmet on the record: no intervention is recorded as responding and the Electoral Code's biometric provisions have a proposed status of adopted, and these statuses are themselves proposals for G6. What remains is an assessment of the Code against data protection law and proper oversight of personal data used in campaigns. The State Election Commission addressed some irregularities, but that does not reach these two points, and this finding rests on evidence no newer than 2023.
The Commission raised it only in 2022 and 2023, it is not in the main findings, and it is peripheral to the data theme.
